title: Call of Duty®: Black Ops
text: Campaign/Zombies Review Quite simply, this game has one of the best campaign plots I've ever seen. The 1960's, CIA Black Ops in Russia and the Vietnam War, conspiracies, and a diabolical political plot to topple nations... all taken seriously in a totally immersive and epic experience. The gameplay is varied, indoors and outdoors, from lush tropical jungles to intelligence headquarters buildings, in a number of different historical conflicts. No spoilers, but the whole story is about finding a hidden, classified truth that is as mindblowing as the warheads that threaten to destroy the world. This dynamic and interesting campaign is unmatched, certainly throughout the Call of Duty series, as well as all the games I've played. It may not be the newest game, but the plot is worth it, I guarantee. Although the plot and story elements alone are enough to warrant a purchase, it is as fun of an ADS FPS as I've ever played, with decent graphics, punchy weapons, and great levels. I've played through the entire game on Veteran Difficulty, the most challenging difficulty, and had an absolute blast. There's not an overwhelming amount of collectables, and they remain found after multiple playthroughs. The Zombies mode in this game is also great, probably better than Black Ops 2. It's not overly complicated like its sequel, and is just solid and hardy. I'm terrible at Zombies and still loved it. In one level you actually get to play as John F. Kennedy fighting zombies in the US Pentagon. Awesome? Awesome. One of my favorites! This isn't a review for the multiplayer, but it is also spectacular and they come together when you get black ops.

title: Call of Juarez™
text: This is an excellent but short FPS along the lines of Half Life, but in a faithful western setting. While old, it has aged well and runs completely bug free in 4K under Windows 10.   Numerous graphics settings round out the PC-first ethic of the developers. Gameplay is novel, with two protagonists (each level has you controlling one of the two), each with different strengths and weaknesses.  While this could have just been a gimmick it was implemented in such a way that you can enjoy the strengths of each character without being frustrated by their limits. Great level design gives you multiple paths to achieve the same outcome, and excellent re-use of assets stretches the game out from the (admittedly short) 15 hours it took me to finish. A few small gripes - the "quickdraw" duel mechanic is janky and annoying.   Some of the puzzles are obtuse.  The game is dated (but has aged well).    These aren't showstoppers, however.

text: I really wanted to like this one because I loved the sequel (Bound in Blood), which I played first. Overall, the production values were great. Voice acting, art style, story, etc. Switching between characters on both sides of the fence also made for interesting gamplay styles and narrative. However, some of the gameplay mechanics are very flawed. Random difficulty spikes and changes in mechanics like fist fighting weren't really fun. There are some stretches of the game where you have to go a long time without heath pickups, and whether you take damage or not is dependent on a random dice roll of whether or not enemies hit your armor or head. The maps are generally linear but whenever new path ways open up, it's not always evident where you are supposed to backtrack to find a new path. This leads to a lot of wandering around, and if you are in a sequence where you have a time limit, finding out where you need to go may lead to failure. There are also stuck in geometry problems if you wander off the the path. It was probably great at the time it was new but it  seems like the game didn't age very well by today's standards. By the end it felt like a boring (but very difficult) slog. I'm still glad I got to get closure on this story, but if you are interested in a western themed shooter, play the sequel Bound in Blood first, and then decide whether you want to play this one to get the full story. The sequel is actually a prequel story-wise, so you don't really lose anything by playing them out of order, in my opinion. Playing this one really made me appreciate the sequel. The devs learned many lessons and improved upon pretty much every gameplay aspect.

title: Call of Juarez™
text: A peculiar cycle of games, the Call of Juarez series was one of the more thoughtful FPS shooters to be produced in many years.   The first game was a prequal to the second, using  a very post modernist way to tell its backstory. Well designed, Call of Juarez has an intuitive game system and graphics engine, no doubt. Despite the valleylike walls of the settings, which make the levels feel like open mazes, the environments are  pleasing tothe eye. The shooting dynamics are well implemented. Billy's whip and Ray's excellent handling of guns are interesting new features. However, the stealth chapters of the story tend deprive players of having more of a chance to have firefights, which is remedied later on in the game, but only in the final chapter. Also, interactions with NPC's of the chapters is reduced to a minimum, leading to the impression that there isn't much human involvement beyond the strictly necessary. Call of Juarez is a useful case study and a compelling adventure, though it was a new breed of animal in its infancy. The game has to be appreciated for all that it's got, not the elements that sometimes don't feel satisfying or complete enough.

title: Call of Juarez™
text: Call of Juarez is a Western FPS, which you don't see too often. Unfortunately, it's a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one. Most of that is because of the gameplay. You alternate between playing Billy, a stupid and annoying Mexican kid, and Ray, who's essentially a religious, gunslinging version of Batman from The Dark Knight Returns. As Billy, you do stealth and Indiana Jones-style whip-assisted platforming, both of which are janky as ♥♥♥♥ and at times completely don't work. Sometimes I'd spend five minutes trying to get past one jump because of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rope physics, and the less said about the stealth, the better. Also, your health pool is a joke and literally anything can kill you. As Ray, you do shooting where the amount of damage it takes to kill specific enemies seems to be completely random and you have to reload every five seconds for far too long. Sometimes you're One-Hit McGee who can kill twelve enemies in a row before reloading, and other times one guy manages to eat five bullets and dodge seven more, making you reload both revolvers for what seems like a full minute before trying again while he and his friends take potshots at you. Eventually, cover becomes more common and you get less unusable guns, but it's still not a fun process. Things get bad enough near the end that every single enemy starts dropping a health potion when they die, which seems like the wrong way to go about fixing the issue. Still, it's better than ♥♥♥♥in' Billy. But don't worry, there's a whole slew of other ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanics for both characters! Ray can kick down doors, which feels completely weightless and ineffectual and I think gets used all of twice. There's a weapon durability mechanic where a brand-new gun can break down to the point that it explodes in your hands over the course of a single level. There are dueling and fistfight minigames that you have to do occasionally, both of which ♥♥♥♥ing suck. You also ride barely-steerable horses sometimes. There's also some ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous fall damage. Come to think of it, nothing except blindly firing a shotgun at an enemy feels good to do in this game. To complement the travesty that is the basic gameplay, the story is mostly a slog. It's completely forgettable by itself, but it's mostly told by a metric ♥♥♥♥-ton of expository dialogue in lengthy cutscenes placed directly after save points, so if you die you get to watch them all over again. To be fair, the game's not completely without its good points. You can see your whole body if you look down, which I always like. The sound design is generally good, and there are some impressively large environments and a few pretty good setpieces. The game is weirdly enamored with physically simulating everything that isn't nailed down, from dead snakes to your whip to your corpse when you die. This doesn't mean anything in gameplay terms, but it can be entertaining. That's about it for good stuff. So yes, Call of Juarez is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's unpleasant to play in every aspect, and any redeeming qualities it has are comparatively quite minor. I only really hated playing it several times throughout the whole thing, but the rest of the time I was filled with vague, omnipresent distaste. If you like it for some reason, great, but please don't go telling me about it.

title: Call of Juarez™
text: Before Dead Island brought Techland to the spotlight, they'd actually already released the fantastic Call of Juarez. Let's start with the negatives; the loading times are atrocious. I mean, you could probably fire up the game, go to the bathroom and take a dump and be back in time just to see the last centimeter of the loading bar filling up. The other negative is a technical issue, there's no option for vsync and it has to be forced on via d3doverdriver. I wasn't able to force it via AMD's CCC. Another negative would be the horse controls, not the best, but a good effort for a game from 2006. Now the positives; the story is a classic western tale. A young man comes home after months of searching for treasure and isn't exactly given a warm welcome. It only gets worse when he arrives at his farm to find his mother and step father dead. Billy is one of two protagonists, the other being Reverand Ray, the brother of Billy's step father. Switching between the two characters throughout the various episodes during the duration of the game sets up brilliant pacing with the story. As Ray hunts down Billy, believing he murdered his brother and in-law, you'll come across bandits and apache, various landscape of the massive western USA. From mountains and valleys, to the heat stricken Mexico. It's quite the adventure. What I really liked about the gameplay was the change in tone, Billy, being a slimmer character and less hardened, used stealth to sneak through levels, while Ray is the run and gun type while taking cover and strategizing. That's about it. 9/10

title: Castle Crashers®
text: I received Castle Crashers as a gift from an old friend some years ago, and didn’t get around to finishing it until just yesterday. Its a 90s-style beat-em-up for up to four player coop both local and online, originally featured on Xbox Live Arcade before finding its true home here on PC. While they recommend that you use an Xbox controller, I can safely say that using a keyboard is much more responsive and in the long run will save you some frustration. Combat is fast and frenetic and you can quickly find yourself stunlocked into oblivion, so it is important to learn the game’s exceedingly simple but egregiously spamable combos so that you screw over your enemies harder then they could ever do to you. It’s also one of those games where ordinary packs of enemies are more dangerous then bosses, mostly due to their numbers and worse, a lack of mook chivalry- everything that can attack you at once, WILL attack you at once. I believe I initially left off of the campaign out of frustration over its apparent difficulty, though I now understand that what I thought was legitimate challenge was really just a lot of cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, which I was able to overcome by cheesing the game right back. That said, I enjoyed Castle Crashers’ bizarre art style, colorful palette and responsive controls, as well as its rather large range of characters and weapons. I completed a playthrough as the green knight with a focus on strength and defense, which proved a reltively safe and reliable approach. There is a dizzying lineup of unlockable characters, some of which require at least two playthroughs to acquire. While readily enjoyable alone once one learns how to play, Castle Crashers is an experience best shared with others in coop multiplayer.

title: Castle of Illusion
text: Castle of Illusion is a great game. I would even say it's one of the best platformers I've played this year. You play as Mickey who has to save his beloved Minnie from an evil witch, and collect as many gems and other special items along the way. There are also special unlockable costumes for Mickey to be found as well. The aesthetics are gorgeous, leaving us with a very colorful game. The music fits the mood very well. The narrator, as well as the voice actor for other characters, do a great job at their respective roles. The cutscenes are played out in a lovely 2D hand drawn style, almost like reading a story book. And don't let the fact that it's a Mickey Mouse game catch you off guard. Castle of Illusion is in no way a game only kids would enjoy. There's plenty of challenge for all ages, especially if you're trying to 100% clear it. Overall, it's a must play for any Disney fan, and even if you don't like Disney or Mickey Mouse too much, it's still worth a look.
